conflict_notes: Temperature: Penn State says 92 to 95 F (95 F in its brooding guide), UNH says 90 to 95 F, Merck gives 85 to 90 F at floor level. Protein: Penn State and Oregon State say 18 to 20%, Poultry Extension, Alabama Extension and My Pet Chicken say 20 to 22%. Space: 1/4 vs 1/2 sq ft.
brooder_temp_notes: Measured at chick height under the heat. Warm the brooder at least 24 hours before chicks arrive. Leave a cooler area so chicks can move away from the heat.
space_notes: Penn State lists 1/4 sq ft per chick for week 1. Minnesota lists 1/2 sq ft per chick from day 1 to 6 weeks.
feed_type: Chick starter (crumble or finely milled mash). Medicated or non-medicated.
water_notes: Have water ready before chicks arrive. Dip each chick's beak in the water as you place it in the brooder so it finds the drinker. Use a chick waterer that chicks cannot drown in. For bantams, marbles or pebbles in the tray stop drowning.

grit.type: None while chicks eat only chick starter. Offer chick grit as soon as they get anything else.

heat_lamp_or_plate: Heat lamp: hang by a chain, not the cord, and keep it at least 20 inches from anything flammable. Use a porcelain socket and a guard. Heat plate: chicks warm up by touching it, the surface stays around 125 F or less, and fire risk is much lower. Follow the maker's height settings.

can_go_outside.notes: Chicks cannot control their body temperature yet.

milestones: Chicks absorb the yolk just before hatching. It can carry them for about 48 to 72 hours, which is why day-old chicks can be shipped.
Sex-link chicks can be sexed by down colour at hatch. A few strains can be feather sexed. Most breeds cannot be sexed by eye yet.

common_problems.name: Chilling or overheating
common_problems.what_to_do: Watch the chicks, not just the thermometer. Huddled under the heat and loud peeping means too cold. Spread far from the heat, in the corners, means too hot. Evenly spread and quietly busy means right.

common_problems.name: Pasty butt (pasted vent)
common_problems.what_to_do: Check vents daily. Soften the dried droppings with warm water and clean them off gently. A dab of petroleum jelly helps stop it sticking again. Fix the cause: a brooder that is too cold or too hot, crowding, or shipping stress.

common_problems.name: Splay leg (spraddle leg)
common_problems.what_to_do: Use a grippy floor such as paper towel or pine shavings, never newspaper. Caught early, a soft hobble that holds the legs under the body for a day or two often corrects it.

common_problems.name: Piling and smothering
common_problems.what_to_do: Chicks pile up when cold or frightened. Check the heat, round off corners with a chick guard, and keep drafts out.

tasks: Set up and test the brooder a day ahead.
Dip each beak in water, then show them the feed.
Check every vent for pasting.
Use paper towel or a grippy liner over shavings for the first days, not newspaper.
Put a chick guard around the heat to stop drafts and piling in corners.

common_problems.name: Coccidiosis
common_problems.what_to_do: Signs are a hunched, fluffed-up chick, low energy, and loose or watery droppings, sometimes with blood. Keep litter dry and waterers clean. Amprolium in medicated starter helps prevent it, and amprolium in the water is the usual treatment. Call a vet or extension office if chicks are sick.

common_problems.name: Feather pecking and cannibalism
common_problems.what_to_do: Give more space as birds grow, keep lights dim rather than bright white, give them things to scratch at, and remove any bird with an open wound until it heals.

tasks: Check droppings daily for loose, watery or bloody stools.
Keep the litter dry, especially around drinkers.

space_notes: Merck: 1.5 to 2 sq ft inside plus 8 to 10 sq ft of run per hen. Minnesota: up to 2 1/2 sq ft for mature birds.
feed_type: Layer feed, free choice, with oyster shell in a separate dish.
water_notes: Hens need constant water to keep laying. Stop it freezing in winter.

grit.type: Hen-size insoluble grit, plus free-choice oyster shell for calcium. Oyster shell is not grit.

milestones: Most hens start laying between 18 and 24 weeks. Heavy breeds and bantams can take 6 months or more.
Peak lay is around 35 weeks, at more than 9 eggs per 10 hens a day (Oregon State).
Early eggs may be small or odd-shaped. This usually settles in the first month.

common_problems.name: Thin or soft shells
common_problems.what_to_do: Check the hens are on layer feed and offer oyster shell free choice.

common_problems.name: Vent prolapse or egg binding
common_problems.what_to_do: Isolate the hen and call a vet. Balanced layer feed with enough calcium lowers the risk.

common_problems.name: Winter laying stops
common_problems.what_to_do: Hens need about 14 hours of light to keep laying. Add light in the morning on a timer if you want winter eggs.

tasks: Switch to layer feed at the first egg.
Offer oyster shell in its own dish.
Collect eggs at least twice a day.
